name: Sardines
summary: Sardines are small oily fish eaten fresh or from a tin, often with their soft bones. This page lists what people say sardines do; each claim can be checked against the research when you choose. No clear ancient health claims about sardines were found.
inIt: The UK food table (CoFID) measures raw sardine flesh at 134 kcal, 6.1 g of fat, 19.8 g of protein, 4 µg of vitamin D, 8.3 µg of vitamin B12 and 1.11 g of EPA and DHA (omega-3 fats) per 100 g. Tinned in brine and drained, with the soft bones, it has 679 mg of calcium per 100 g against 50 mg in the raw flesh. The table does not measure the many other compounds in fish.

Like other fish, sardines can build up histamine if they spoil: a study of retail sardine and mackerel found histamine-producing bacteria in most sardines tested and histamine in the muscle of fish carrying them.

tableFoods.label: 1 small tin of sardines in brine, drained (about 90 g)

processing: Tinning changes what is eaten: drained tinned sardines have 679 mg of calcium per 100 g in the UK food table because the bones are eaten, against 50 mg in raw flesh, and 368 mg of sodium in brine against 136 mg raw.

whoShouldBeCareful.note: Fish allergy can cause severe reactions, including fatal anaphylaxis, and often lasts into adulthood. A review also lists scombroid poisoning (a reaction to histamine in spoiled fish) among non-allergic reactions to fish. If you react to fish, talk to your doctor or an allergist.

unknowns: Whether eating sardines changes health outcomes in people: this page does not review those studies.
How much histamine or contaminant a given tin or fresh fish holds: it varies with handling and source.
Ancient writers: Athenaeus and Aristotle discuss fish called sardines by name, but the passages that were read describe names and types, not health uses; nothing about the body was found.
